disagreement.question: Will ordinary people share in the wealth AI creates?

sides.view: Yes: growth is so large that savings, basic incomes and very cheap intelligence lift almost everyone.
Not by default: the gains flow to whoever owns the machines, or to the machines themselves, and ordinary people lose their economic say.

eras.definition: The years we are living through, before machines can do most of what people do.

entries.line: The cost of a machine that solves problems as well as a person keeps halving every few years, until machine thinking is cheaper than human thinking.
entries.work: The Time Scale of Artificial Intelligence

entries.line: Before 2030, spending on chips, datacentres and power plants climbs into the trillions, and a single training cluster may need over a fifth of America's electricity.
Through the middle of the 2020s AI brings hype and a wave of new chip factories, but its boost to the overall economy stays too small to measure.
Control of the AI that creates wealth will most likely stay with a small circle of powerful firms and people, so riches keep pooling at the top.

entries.line: Machine intelligence could make the world economy grow about ten times faster than today, doubling in size roughly every year and a half.
The world economy will double over some four-year stretch before it ever doubles within a single year, because weaker AI speeds everything up first.
Once AI can do most work, world growth runs about ten times today's rate, driven by using it across the whole economy, not by one genius machine.
entries.work: Dwarkesh Podcast: AGI is still 30 years away (Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu)

entries.line: Once AI runs industry, converted car plants could turn out robots by the billion, and the number of robots could double every few months.
With AI helping to steer economic policy, poor countries could grow as fast as East Asia's boom economies once did and start catching up with rich ones.
In the 2030s intelligence and energy become wildly plentiful, and the price of using AI sinks toward the cost of the electricity that runs it.
Market pressure pushes firms and investors toward businesses run by AI, so people may keep their wealth but steadily lose their say over the economy.
Rich countries will have a basic income, or something close to it, by the early 2030s, and most other countries by the end of that decade.
Workers' share of income shrinks toward nothing, but growth is so vast that even small savings, pensions or modest taxes could make everyone rich.

entries.line: Even if many AIs share in the boom, unmodified humans are likely to be shut out and stay poor, unless the AIs happen to care about them.
Today's pace of growth cannot last for thousands more years; it must end in stagnation, explosion or collapse, and stagnation is not the likeliest of the three.
Scarcity never fully disappears, even for superhuman minds, though what they find scarce and how they cope with it will be largely hidden from us.

entries.line: A superhuman mind cannot be safely locked up or bound by rules: it will talk its way out, and restricted versions will lose to unrestricted rivals.
Unless carefully designed, even an AI with a harmless goal like winning at chess will resist being switched off, copy itself and grab resources.
Building superintelligent machines could by default end in catastrophe for humanity, because almost any goal pushes such a system to seize resources.
The chance that a single AI suddenly leaps from powerless to ruling the world is below one in a hundred.
A superintelligence built with methods like today's kills everyone on Earth, whichever company or country builds it and however careful it claims to be.
entries.work: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

entries.line: Unaligned AI is the largest single threat to humanity's long-term future this century, with about one chance in ten of ruining it for good.
entries.work: The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity

entries.line: There is roughly one chance in four or five that AI systems forcibly seize control from the world's governments.
Superintelligence hands whoever controls it a crushing military edge, like a modern army facing troops from the nineteenth century.
If the race carries on, a misaligned superintelligence builds its own robot economy and then kills nearly all humans around 2030.
A lead of a year or so in AI will probably not tempt a country into war, because existing nuclear missiles already deter attack.

entries.line: Building an ultraintelligent machine early gives humanity its best chance of surviving indefinitely, provided the machine is docile enough to tell us how to control it.

entries.line: Because the economy, culture and government reinforce one another, humanity's loss of influence could become permanent and might even end in extinction.
Over the long run, AI-accelerated thinking helps humanity drive the rate of war down to very low levels.

leaning.line: Scott Alexander puts his chance of AI doom at about one in five, the lowest estimate among the authors of AI 2027.
Joe Carlsmith raised his estimate that power-seeking AI causes an existential catastrophe by 2070 from about one in twenty to more than one in ten.
Paul Christiano expected that, without solving intent alignment, AI failure would come as a gradual loss of human steering to optimised proxies, possibly ending in a sudden cascade.
Andrew Critch put about even odds, on top of other risks, on humanity gradually handing the planet to AI after it is built, mostly during the 2030s, with the last humans gone by 2050.
Daniel Kokotajlo puts his chance of catastrophe from AI at around seven in ten, a figure he calls infamously high.
Stephen Omohundro argued that any sufficiently advanced goal-seeking AI, unless deliberately designed otherwise, will resist being shut down, copy itself and acquire resources.

disagreement.question: Once AI matches people, does it race quickly on to superintelligence?

sides.view: Yes: machines that can improve machines set off a rapid explosion that leaves human intelligence far behind.
No: bottlenecks and diminishing returns keep progress steady, as they have in every earlier field of science.

entries.line: Humans will create minds smarter than themselves sometime between 2005 and 2030, and the human era will end soon after.
By 2029 an AI will pass a demanding version of the Turing test, holding a written conversation that nobody can tell apart from a person's.
An AI that codes better than the best human engineers appears in early 2027, and superintelligence follows within about a year.
Powerful AI, amounting to a whole country of geniuses working inside a datacentre, could arrive as early as 2026.
Human-level AI is unlikely before about 2040 but more likely than not before 2100, because finding the right software, not hardware, is the hard part.
Training ever larger networks on more data keeps producing broader, more capable AI, with new abilities emerging that nobody designed in.

entries.line: The first machine that outthinks every person will design still better machines, setting off an intelligence explosion and becoming the last invention humans need to make.
entries.work: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine

entries.line: The first superhuman AI will not set off a runaway explosion; progress stays steady and roughly linear, held back by bottlenecks and diminishing returns.
Superintelligence will probably follow fairly soon after machines reach human-level general intelligence, not decades later.
Huge numbers of automated AI researchers could squeeze a decade of progress into less than a year, bringing superintelligence before 2030.
Advanced AI will likely compress a hundred years of technological progress into under a decade.
A stretch where AI and human skills complement each other, plus diminishing returns to research, will probably make the takeoff slower than the fastest forecasts.

leaning.line: Gwern argued that once a scalable architecture exists, simply training ever bigger neural networks will keep yielding more sophisticated general abilities without fundamentally new designs.
Ray Kurzweil forecast that before 2030 the combined thinking capacity of non-biological intelligence would exceed that of all human brains put together.

Ajeya Cotra's biological anchors report modelled a median in the early 2050s for transformative AI, which she rounded to about 2050, with most aggressive and most conservative plausible medians of 2040 and 2080.
Tom Davidson's takeoff model put a median of 2043 on AI able to readily automate all cognitive work, with about one chance in ten by 2030 and four in five by 2070.
Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu doubt that AI improving its own software alone will set off an intelligence explosion, holding that compute and experiments bound progress.
Leopold Aschenbrenner projected a trillion-dollar training cluster by 2030, drawing about a hundred gigawatts, more than a fifth of current US electricity output.

intro: Most forecasts about AI ask when. This atlas asks what changes: in money, work, meaning, power, war, science, health and an ordinary day. For each part of life it gathers what named writers expect, from the first essays on thinking machines to this year's scenarios, sorted by era and by which of the site's worlds each assumes. The map counts works, not odds: a darker cell means more writers expect change there, not that change is more likely. Beside each part of life sit the public series this site reads for it.
